question.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(x-1)+1}{x-1})}^{3x-3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x-1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{3n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$
